article.title: TinyGo 0.42 Makes Runtime Panics Recoverable, Adds a UEFI Target and a Seeed Studio Starter Kit
article.summary: TinyGo 0.42 finally lets defer/recover catch runtime panics and adds a minimal UEFI target; a week later the project shipped its first official hardware kit, built around Seeed Studio's XIAO ESP32-C3.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

TinyGo, the LLVM-based Go compiler for microcontrollers and WebAssembly, shipped [version 0.42](https://tinygo.org/blog/2026/tinygo-0.42-recover-is-real/) on September 1, 2026, headlined by long-awaited support for recovering from runtime panics. Eight days later, the project followed up with its first official hardware bundle, the [TinyGo Starter Kit with Seeed Studio XIAO](https://tinygo.org/blog/2026/tinygo-starter-kit-with-xiao/), pairing a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-C3 board with a set of plug-in sensor modules and a tutorial series.

## What We Know

### Recoverable panics close a gap with "Big" Go

According to [TinyGo's release announcement](https://tinygo.org/blog/2026/tinygo-0.42-recover-is-real/), version 0.42 "closes one of the oldest gaps between TinyGo and 'Big' Go" by making runtime panics recoverable. Previously, the team wrote, "a nil pointer dereference or a divide by zero in a TinyGo program was the end of the story" — the program simply stopped. Now: "Nil pointer dereferences, divide by zero, out of range slice and map operations, and channel panics all are handled through defer and recover the way you expect them to." A vectored exception handler covers the same behavior on Windows, and `recover` now works on riscv64 as well. Fatal conditions such as out-of-memory errors remain unrecoverable, "because there is nothing you can really do about it," the post notes. The change also fixed the standard library's `testing` package, which now supports `Goexit`, `SkipNow`, and `FailNow` — unblocking "a large number of standard library test suites."

### Go 1.27, LLVM 22, and a new UEFI target

The release adds support for Go 1.27, including its new generic-methods feature, and moves TinyGo's own builds to LLVM 22 while keeping LLVM 19 and LLVM 20 working for people who build from a distribution package, according to the [release announcement](https://tinygo.org/blog/2026/tinygo-0.42-recover-is-real/). The [GitHub release notes](https://github.com/tinygo-org/tinygo/releases/tag/v0.42.0) count more than 240 commits to the main repository since the prior release. TinyGo 0.42 also introduces a minimal UEFI target, letting a compiled Go program run "as a UEFI application before any operating system starts," with support for UEFI time and events and goroutines enabled through a default task scheduler. The team describes the UEFI work as "early," adding "there is a lot still to do."

### Hardware support widens

The release brings a round of chip and board additions. ESP32 gains interrupt support, an ADC driver, and flash execute-in-place (XIP), plus WiFi through the espradio package and Bluetooth support on the ESP32-C3 and ESP32-S3, per the [release announcement](https://tinygo.org/blog/2026/tinygo-0.42-recover-is-real/). The [GitHub release notes](https://github.com/tinygo-org/tinygo/releases/tag/v0.42.0) add that the newer ESP32-C6 chip gets a minimal implementation with I2C and ADC support. STM32 users get a new OTG FS USB driver for the F4 and F7 families, support for the STM32H7 and NUCLEO-H753ZI board, and support for the STM32U031 chip. Other new hardware includes Puya PY32F microcontrollers, the Pimoroni Blinky 2350 and Badger 2350 boards, and a "Plus" variant of the Seeed Studio XIAO nRF52840, while USB endpoint registration across the RP2, SAMD21, SAMD51, and nRF52840 platforms becomes dynamic and bidirectional.

### A first official starter kit

On September 9, TinyGo announced the [Starter Kit with Seeed Studio XIAO](https://tinygo.org/blog/2026/tinygo-starter-kit-with-xiao/), calling it "the first official TinyGo starter kit." The box contains a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-C3 — "a RISC-V board roughly the size of a postage stamp" with 2.4GHz WiFi and BLE radios built in — a Grove Base for XIAO that removes the need for breadboard wiring, and eleven Grove peripheral modules split across three categories: sensing (button, touch, rotary angle, light, sound, temperature, vibration, and acceleration), action (a buzzer and an RGB LED stick), and display (an OLED screen). TinyGo's other XIAO-family boards — the ESP32-S3, nRF52840, RP2040, RP2350, and SAMD21 — can substitute for the ESP32-C3 in the kit "without you changing anything else," the team said. A companion tutorial series, written by TinyGo core team member Patricio Whittingslow, walks through installation, digital and analog inputs, the display, and wireless communication. The team credited Seeed Studio for "working alongside us to figure out what belongs" in the kit, and noted the pun behind the partnership: "'Xiao' actually means 'Tiny' in Chinese."

## What We Don't Know

TinyGo's announcement of the starter kit does not list a price. The team also flagged the new UEFI target as "early work" without specifying a timeline for expanding it beyond its current minimal time, event, and scheduler support.
